subtitle.en: Matric year: choosing courses, applications and NSFAS

blurb.en: Choosing a course, application fees, funding forms and results day. About 5 minutes.

text.en: Applications open soon. You love one subject, another course pays better, and your marks fit a third. Everyone has an opinion.

outcome.en: You choose the subject you'd study for free. Now check what its graduates actually do.
The salary looks good on paper. Four years is a long time in a course you don't enjoy.
The advisor shows you courses that fit your marks, your interests and the job market.

tip.en: University career offices and open days answer questions from learners too.

title.en: Your friends are all applying to one university

text.en: Your whole group is applying to the same university. It doesn't offer your first-choice course, but you wouldn't be alone.

outcome.en: You apply where your friends apply. You'll arrive knowing someone, in your second-choice course.
You compare courses, costs and distance. One university fits you better than it fits your friends.
It costs one more application fee, and it keeps both doors open.

text.en: Outside the internet café, a man offers to do your university and NSFAS applications for R150. He needs your ID number and a password. You have {money}.

outcome.en: He takes the R150 and your details, and nothing is ever submitted. Now a stranger has your ID number and your password.

tip.en: Applying is something you do yourself, on official websites. If this happens, change your passwords and tell your school.

outcome.en: It takes an afternoon and a lot of scanning. Every reference number and password is yours alone.
Your LO teacher sits with you at the school computer. You apply yourself, on the official websites, and it costs nothing.

title.en: Your family wants you closer to home

text.en: Your family wants you to study close to home, or to choose the course an uncle recommends. They're worried, and they're also paying attention.

outcome.en: Home is happier. You wonder about the course you didn't choose.
You show them the costs, the funding and how often you'd come home. They agree to one application further away.
You apply where you planned. Supper is quiet for a week, then your mother asks about res.

text.en: Each application costs about R200, and closing dates are different everywhere. You have {money}.

outcome.en: One fee, one form, and everything rides on it.
It costs R600, and you have three chances instead of one.
Some universities don't charge for online applications, and others waive the fee if you ask. You apply to three for R200.

tip.en: Ask each university about application fee waivers before you pay.

text.en: The NSFAS form wants a signed consent form from a parent, and the name on your ID doesn't match your school records.

outcome.en: The application sits as "incomplete" for weeks. You only find out in January.
It takes two trips and an affidavit. Your details match, and the form goes through.

tip.en: A police station can commission an affidavit for free, and your school can certify copies of your documents.

outcome.en: Your LO teacher helps you upload the consent form and check every detail against your ID.

tip.en: Missing documents are the most common reason funding applications stall. Check your status after you submit.

text.en: While you wait for results, you look for a room. A page called "Student Rooms Near Campus" says spaces are almost gone: send R300 today to hold one. You have {money}.

outcome.en: The page takes your R300 and blocks you. No real residence asks for a holding fee by message before you have seen a lease.

tip.en: "Pay today or lose it" is the warning sign. Only pay into an account you can match to the university or an accredited provider.

outcome.en: You apply on the university's own website, before the closing date. Res applications close early, often months before classes start.
The accommodation office sends its list of accredited private residences. The page asking for R300 is not on it.

tip.en: If you are on NSFAS, private accommodation must be accredited or your rent won't be paid. Check the list before you sign anything.

text.en: Your matric results are out, and they're lower than you expected. Your first-choice course needed a few more APS points.

outcome.en: You switch off your phone for two days. When you switch it back on, the choices are still waiting for you.
You still qualify for your second choice, and for an extended programme in your first.

tip.en: Each university's website lists the minimum APS points for every course. Call or email the admissions office to confirm your options.

label.en: Rewrite, and apply again next year

outcome.en: You won't start university this year. You'll rewrite the subjects you need, and apply again next year for the course you really want.

tip.en: Ask your school how to register for the supplementary or Second Chance exams, and when registration closes. Then check when applications for next year open.

text.en: Your phone is back on. Your first-choice course is out of reach this year, but other doors haven't closed. What now?

outcome.en: You check the APS points: you still qualify for your second choice. You accept the offer before it closes.

tip.en: Each university lists the minimum APS points for every course. Call or email admissions to confirm before the offer closes.

label.en: Look for something that fits better

outcome.en: Admissions points you to an extended programme in your first-choice course: one extra year, and the same degree at the end.

tip.en: Extended programmes add a foundation year for students who were a few APS points short. Ask admissions whether you qualify.

label.en: Rewrite, and apply again next year

outcome.en: You won't start university this year. You'll rewrite the subjects you need, and apply again next year for the course you really want.

tip.en: Ask your school how to register for the supplementary or Second Chance exams, and when registration closes. Then check when applications for next year open.

text.en: The one university you applied to has put you on a waiting list. Classes start in five weeks.

outcome.en: You plan a year of work and reapplying. A gap year with a plan is not a failure.
A TVET college near you offers a related qualification, with funding. It's a real route, not a consolation prize.

tip.en: TVET colleges take applications on their websites or at the campus, and NSFAS funds TVET students too.

outcome.en: You register with the national clearing house for late applications and call the faculty. A space opens.

tip.en: Ask your school or the higher education department about the clearing house for applicants without a place.

text.en: "We are pleased to offer you a place." You read it four times, then send a screenshot to everyone you know.
A university has an online "day in the life" you can try before you choose.

outcome.en: Now you know which questions to ask at the open day.
It stays in your tabs. Applications close in three weeks.

text.en: A parent asks how much university will really cost. You're not sure.

outcome.en: Fees, rent, food, transport: seeing the total makes the plan real.
They nod, but they're still worried. So are you.

text.en: You'll be living away from home. Do you know what the room comes with, and what you must bring?

outcome.en: The residence office, or your landlord, sends it: bring bedding, a lock, plates and a pot. It also says which appliances aren't allowed.
You arrive with a kettle you can't use and no bedding. Res WhatsApp groups sell second-hand basics cheaply.
